title: Simple chain-loop edging
subtitle: A row of looped scallops to trim any straight edge
excerpt: A plain, quick edging: one firm row of double crochet, then a row of chain loops that arch into soft scallops. Worked here as a standalone strip in 4-ply cotton, it is the gentlest introduction to crochet trims and lengthens to fit any edge.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the simplest of the looped crochet edgings worked along a base row. Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The yarn weight, hook size, and gauge are modernised; the loop structure is Victorian.

crochet.gaugeText: 16 double crochet to 10 cm in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. Gauge is not critical for an edging, but a looser or tighter tension changes the finished length.
crochet.finishedSizeText: About 12 cm long and 3 cm deep as written. Lengthen by adding chains to the foundation in multiples of 3.

glossaryTerms.definition: The starting row of chain stitches that the first row of stitches is worked into. Its length sets the length of the edging.
A short, firm crochet stitch with no yarn-over before the hook goes in. Called single crochet in the United States.
Wetting or steaming a finished piece and pinning it to shape while it dries, so the stitches settle even and the loops sit open.

content.text: This is the plainest crochet trim: a firm base row, then a row of chain loops that arch into soft scallops. It is worked here as a short standalone strip so you can practise the rhythm, then lengthen it to edge a face cloth, a shelf, or the hem of a simple bag. The pattern is written in UK terms, where double crochet is the short, firm stitch (called single crochet in the United States).
About 15 m makes the strip as written, with plenty to spare. A smooth mercerised cotton such as Scheepjes Catona shows the loops cleanly. Any 4-ply cotton works.
The usual pairing for 4-ply cotton. If your tension runs loose, drop to 2.75 mm.
For weaving in the two tails at the end.

16 double crochet to 10 cm in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. Gauge is not critical for an edging, but a looser or tighter tension changes the finished length, so check it if the strip must reach a set measurement.
dc = double crochet (UK), called single crochet in the US
Read the chart alongside the written rows below. The chart shows the shape of the loops; the written rows give the stitch counts.
in the 2nd chain from the hook, then 1 dc in each of the next 18 chains. (19 sts)
Ch 1 and turn. Work 1 dc in the first dc. [Ch 5, skip 2 dc, 1 dc in the next dc] 6 times. This makes 6 chain loops sitting between 7 anchor stitches. (7 sts)
Fasten off, leaving a 10 cm tail. The strip is complete.
Weave both tails into the back of the base row with the tapestry needle, doubling back once to lock them, then trim. Pin the strip straight and
it, easing the loops into even arches, and leave it to dry. Blocking is what makes the scallops sit open and regular.

To edge a real piece, work the first row of double crochet straight into the edge of the finished item instead of a foundation chain, keeping the stitch count a multiple of 3 plus 1 so the loops come out even. Longer chain loops give deeper scallops; a picot in the centre of each loop turns the plain trim into a pointed lace edge.
